purpose.intro: Organizations are the module's own tables and services — the identity provider knows nothing about them. Two configs drive every decision: the auth config (membership-keyed standing rules, join-context identifier and consent narrowing) and the org-lifecycle config (create/join policy per org type). The module reads facts and config; it never stores a verdict.

claims.text: **`organization`** — `id`, `type` (org-lifecycle vocabulary, opaque to the module), `name`, `logo`, `metadata`, timestamps.
**`member`** — one row per `(organization, user)` holding `roles` as a `text[]` of scoped role names. The row maps 1:1 to the gate's `MembershipFacts { orgType, roles }` — no translation layer.

**`invitation`** — addressed to exactly one identifier (`email` XOR `phone`, service-validated; no synthetic values), `roles`, a `status` enum (`pending | accepted | rejected | revoked`), `inviterId`, `invitedUserId` (set on accept), and `expiresAt` (stamped at create from the org type's `join.invitation.expiresInSeconds`, default 48h; expiry is computed, never a stored status).

claims.text: Web controls carry a separate marker — `AC(availability-check): <entity>.<action>` — because visibility is not the engine's workstream: controls render for everyone and the server enforces, until availability-check narrows visibility and options from the same rules the engine enforces.

reference.statement: WHO may perform an org action (beyond tenancy — being a member) is the `@prowd/gated-scoped-ac` engine's job, and it is wired: services run the write verdicts (`allowCreate`/`allowUpdate`) and repositories execute engine-resolved scopes through the gated db — `organization.create/read/update`, `member.list/role.update/remove`, `invitation.create/list/revoke`. Permissions live in `configs/access-control`. One known gap stays a service business rule: **role-value escalation** — `member.role.update` and `invitation.create` accept any role literal (the DSL has no cross-role comparison yet).

claims.text: **MembershipService** — `findAllByOrgId`, `updateRoles`, `remove` (both with last-owner protection), `listMemberships` / `listMembershipRoles` (what the session resolves the caller's org-context from), and `setActiveOrganization` (validated against membership; the fact is per-user, in `user_state`).

**InvitationService** — `create` (+ delivery), `listForOrgId`, `revoke`, `getPublicView` (masked, no auth), `findAllByUserIdentifiers`, `accept`, `reject`. Accept **auto-verifies** the invited address — possession was proven by delivery.

**`/organizations` (web) — the platform DIRECTORY**: every org as a managed table (name · type · status badge · search / type / status filters · pagination), with founding a new org from its header. Rows the caller belongs to carry an enter action (activate → the current-org page); foreign rows are read-only — cross-org drill-in arrives with the access-control engine's cross-org read design, never by weakening the active-org session model. The backing `GET /organizations` is engine row-scoped: callers see only the rows their permissions admit (`read_all_organizations_system` for the directory).

**`/my/memberships` + `/my/invitations` (web)**: the caller's memberships — their role per org, LEAVE (self-removal; last-owner protected) — and their pending invitations (accept/decline), each on its own page. Reached from the shell's user menu, which badges the pending-invitation count on the invitations item.

reference.statement: `GET /organizations/:orgId/members` is name-searchable and paginated (`{ rows, total }`). Each row carries the member's profile name/image and their DEFAULT CONTACT (`user_contacts` join — see identifiers.md (`./identifiers.md`)); no provider reads happen on the list path. The web surface renders it as one card: search · a Members/Invitations select · invite (sheet) · the table (name · contact · roles · edit) · pagination; editing opens a sheet (role select + type-to-confirm removal).

claims.text: Reads are row-scoped: an org the context can't read is a **404** on `GET /organizations/:orgId` (not-a-member and not-an-org stay indistinguishable), and a members or invitations list outside the context's scope comes back **empty**. Writes with a row (update, member roles/removal, revoke) are refused with **403** by the update/delete scope. Logo presign has no write of its own, so it probes the same update scope (`findRowsByIdWhereCanUpdate`). Invite has no row at all — a create — so its rules carry a `payload` condition on the invitation being written (`$requestBody.organizationId` is `$session.organization.id`): which org a role may invite into is the access-control config's call, and today every role may invite into its active org only. There is no server-side fallback: a request with no valid header has no context, and no org-scoped permission applies.

Which org a device acts in is the client's memory (the module's web surface keeps last-used in localStorage and defaults to the first membership); the server holds no active-org state at all. The web client sends the active org as the header on EVERY request — it is the context, never the target — so permissions come from the active org's roles only: while acting in A, a member of B sees B only through A's grants (none, today) and switches to B to work in it. A switch removes the org-scoped cached queries and remounts the page (the host's account layout keys its slot on the active org).

The gate excludes `/me` and `/invitations/` so a gated user can still view and accept invitations (accepting an org is exactly how one becomes gated — the loop must not deadlock) and reach `/me/security` to resolve obligations. `/organizations` and everything under it stay gated.

reference.statement: Two inputs, kept apart. The **target** is the org named in the URL — `/organizations/:orgId`, always a real id; the API has no "current" (the web surface's `/organizations/current/…` pages resolve it to the active org's id before calling). The **context** is the caller's **active org** — `session.activeOrganizationId`, the request's claim sent in the `x-active-organization` header and honored only when it names one of the caller's memberships; the scoped-AC bag and role set are built from it. Access control resolves the target against the context: a manager acting in org A reaches only A, and a system admin acting in the system org reads any org's details and members (`read_all_organizations_system`, `read_all_members_system` — read only; managing stays pinned to the active org). Switching is a client-side store write, no endpoint.

claims.text: The app composes its own accept URL from `invitationId`. Absent delivery, invitations are still created (and acceptable via their capability URL); a warning is logged.

This seam carries the invitation OUT to an address, because an invitee may have no account yet. The reply travels the other way: accepting emits `onInvitationAccepted` (see architecture.md (`./architecture.md#lifecycle-hooks--the-outbound-seam`)), which is where the inviter's "X accepted your invitation" comes from. Acceptance is the moment worth announcing precisely because it proves the accepter has an account — a notification can be addressed to a user rather than to a string.

claims.text: The org type's `join.legalConsent` is collected ON the accept page: the public view carries the items paired with their current documents (`joinConsent`), and Accept stays disabled until every mandatory item with a published document is checked — the server re-validates regardless (see legal.md (`./legal.md`)).
Then the gate takes over: the moment the membership exists, the org type's standing rules apply, and anything the org demands that the account doesn't carry yet is collected at `/resolve`.
Founding an org is likewise a signed-in action — there is no register-and-create.

reference.statement: Accepting an invitation is always a **signed-in** action, so a newcomer takes one path: open the invitation link → register (one screen) → return via their intention → accept. The accept seats the membership, re-checks match strictness against the identifiers they now own, records consent against the joined org type, and auto-verifies the invited address (possession was proven by delivery).
